subtopics.title: Calculate relative frequency
subtopics.exposition: The relative frequency of an event is the number of times the event occurs during experimental trials, divided by the total number of trials conducted. The relative frequency is not a theoretical quantity but an experimental one. A positive outcome is an outcome that is in the event set. The relative frequency is the ratio between the number of positive trials and the total number of trials, f = p/t, where p is the number of positive outcomes and t is the total number of trials. To find a relative frequency, repeat the experiment a number of times and count how many times the outcome of the trial is in the event set. To find a relative frequency from an experiment, first identify what one trial is (for example, one soccer match of Team 1 against Team 2). Count the number of positive outcomes: the number of trials in which the event of interest occurs (Team 1 winning occurs 3 times in the 10 matches). Compute the relative frequency as the number of positive outcomes divided by the total number of trials; with 10 trials and 3 wins for Team 1 it is 3/10 = 0.3.

subtopics.title: Compare with theoretical probability
subtopics.exposition: The theoretical probability of an event is a number that can be computed if there is enough information about the experiment; it is different from the observed relative frequency of the event in experimental trials. In general, the relative frequency of an event tends to get closer to the theoretical probability of the event as more trials are performed. After a small number of trials the relative frequency fluctuates a lot around the theoretical probability. As the number of trials increases, the relative frequency fluctuates less and gets closer to the theoretical probability. The more trials run during an experiment, the closer the observed relative frequency of an event will get to the theoretical probability of the event. Keep a running count p of the number of positive outcomes observed after each trial t. Compute the relative frequency after each trial t as f = p/t, using the running count p of positive outcomes, and list the values of f in a table. The relative frequency after all 30 trials is read from the last entry of the table: 13/30 = 0.4 recurring (0.43 to two decimal places). Compare the relative frequency with the theoretical probability: after 30 coin tosses the relative frequency of heads is close to the theoretical probability of 0.5. If each possible outcome in the sample space is equally likely, compute the theoretical probability by counting the number of outcomes in the event set and the number of outcomes in the sample space. When the theoretical probability cannot be computed, use the relative frequency to estimate it, by running experiments and counting the number of positive outcomes. To graph the relative frequencies, plot the number of trials completed, t, on the x-axis and the relative frequency, f, on the y-axis; the theoretical probability is shown as a dashed line.

claims.claim: The relative frequency of an event is the number of times the event occurs during experimental trials, divided by the total number of trials conducted.
The relative frequency is not a theoretical quantity but an experimental one.
To find a relative frequency, repeat the experiment a number of times and count how many times the outcome of the trial is in the event set.
Because the relative frequency is experimental, a different relative frequency is possible every time the experiment is repeated.
The relative frequency depends on the sequence of outcomes observed while doing the statistical experiment.
A positive outcome is an outcome that is in the event set.
The relative frequency is the ratio between the number of positive trials and the total number of trials, f = p/t, where p is the number of positive outcomes and t is the total number of trials.
To find a relative frequency from an experiment, first identify what one trial is (for example, one soccer match of Team 1 against Team 2).
Count the number of positive outcomes: the number of trials in which the event of interest occurs (Team 1 winning occurs 3 times in the 10 matches).
Compute the relative frequency as the number of positive outcomes divided by the total number of trials; with 10 trials and 3 wins for Team 1 it is 3/10 = 0.3.
Keep a running count p of the number of positive outcomes observed after each trial t.
Compute the relative frequency after each trial t as f = p/t, using the running count p of positive outcomes, and list the values of f in a table.
The relative frequency after all 30 trials is read from the last entry of the table: 13/30 = 0.4 recurring (0.43 to two decimal places).
Compare the relative frequency with the theoretical probability: after 30 coin tosses the relative frequency of heads is close to the theoretical probability of 0.5.
In general, the relative frequency of an event tends to get closer to the theoretical probability of the event as more trials are performed.
To graph the relative frequencies, plot the number of trials completed, t, on the x-axis and the relative frequency, f, on the y-axis; the theoretical probability is shown as a dashed line.
After a small number of trials the relative frequency fluctuates a lot around the theoretical probability.
As the number of trials increases, the relative frequency fluctuates less and gets closer to the theoretical probability.

The theoretical probability of an event is a number that can be computed if there is enough information about the experiment; it is different from the observed relative frequency of the event in experimental trials.
If each possible outcome in the sample space is equally likely, compute the theoretical probability by counting the number of outcomes in the event set and the number of outcomes in the sample space.
The more trials run during an experiment, the closer the observed relative frequency of an event will get to the theoretical probability of the event.
In some cases, like the soccer experiment, it is difficult or impossible to compute the theoretical probability of an event.
When the theoretical probability cannot be computed, use the relative frequency to estimate it, by running experiments and counting the number of positive outcomes.
